summary: Updates RFC 5280, the X.509 certificate profile, to align with the 2008 specification for Internationalized Domain Names and to support internationalized email addresses in certificates. It makes name constraints treat ASCII-only and internationalized email addresses the same way. It obsoletes RFC 8399.

plainLanguage.summary: Web addresses and emails can now use letters from many languages. This fixes the rules for certificates, the digital ID cards of websites, so they handle those names correctly.

questions: name constraints for email in certificates
how are idns stored in x.509 certificates
what changed from rfc 8399 to rfc 9549
subtitle: How X.509 certificates carry internationalized domain names and email addresses, with every name stored in its ASCII form.

tldr.problem: RFC 5280 described internationalized names in terms of the 2003 IDN specification, and an earlier fix (RFC 8399) made name constraints for internationalized email hard to implement and led to at least two security vulnerabilities.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9549 replaces several paragraphs of RFC 5280 so that it matches the 2008 IDN specification (IDNA2008), and requires every internationalized domain name to be carried and processed as an A-label, the ASCII form that starts with xn--.
tldr.outcome: Name constraints now treat ASCII-only and internationalized email addresses the same way, mailbox-level constraints are removed, and RFC 8399 is obsoleted.

today: RFC 9549 is a Proposed Standard (Standards Track) published in March 2024. It obsoletes RFC 8399 and updates RFC 5280, and no later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: What This Update Covers
sections.content:
RFC 9549 updates three places in RFC 5280, the X.509 certificate and CRL profile: the Introduction (Section 1), the Name Constraints extension (Section 4.2.1.10), and the processing rules for internationalized names (Section 7). The goal is to align with the 2008 specification for Internationalized Domain Names (IDNs) and to support internationalized email addresses in certificates.

An IDN in Unicode form contains at least one U-label. In certificates, IDNs are carried in ACE-encoded form, meaning every U-label is converted to an A-label. Both IDNA2003 and IDNA2008 use the Punycode algorithm for this conversion. For email, RFC 8398 defines the SmtpUTF8Mailbox form, which lives inside the otherName choice of GeneralName.

Characters in the Unicode category "Symbol, Other" (So), which includes emoji, are not allowed by IDNA2003 or IDNA2008. Some characters allowed by Unicode IDNA Compatibility Processing (UTS #46) are therefore rejected here. For example, a name built on U+1F0A1 (BLACK CHESS KING) fails under this specification but becomes xn--45h.example under UTS #46.
sections.plainLanguage: Some web names have letters from other languages, or even little pictures. Certificates store them in a plain-letter code, and this memo explains the rules. Pictures like emoji are not allowed in these names.

sections.title: Why RFC 8399 Was Replaced
sections.content:
The earlier version of this update, RFC 8399, sometimes required converting A-labels back to U-labels in order to process name constraints for internationalized email addresses. According to RFC 9549, this led to implementation complexity and at least two security vulnerabilities.

The fix is simple to state: now all IDNs are carried and processed as A-labels. RFC 9549 also adds a warning to the Introduction about characters in the "Symbol, Other" category, and it obsoletes RFC 8399.
sections.plainLanguage: The old rule asked computers to flip names back and forth between two spellings, and that made mistakes easy. The new rule keeps everything in one spelling the whole time.

sections.title: Domain Names in Certificates
sections.content:
Section 7.2 of RFC 5280 is replaced in full. IDNs may appear in the subjectAltName and issuerAltName extensions, name constraints, authority and subject information access, CRL distribution points, and issuing distribution point extensions. All of them use GeneralName, whose dNSName field is an IA5String, which is limited to ASCII.

To fit, U-labels are converted to A-labels: the Punycode encoding of the U-label with the ACE prefix xn-- added at the start. Comparisons are strict. Conforming implementations MUST do a case-insensitive exact match on the entire DNS name when comparing names for equality, and a case-insensitive exact match label by label when evaluating name constraints. Any DNS name built by adding labels on the left of the constraint falls inside the constrained subtree.

Implementations that have a user interface SHOULD convert A-labels back to U-labels for display. IDNs also need more memory: an ACE label starts with four extra characters (xn--), and a single international character can take as many as five ASCII characters.

Section 7.3 gets a matching change for domain names written as distinguished names with domainComponent attributes. The old text required the "ToASCII" conversion from RFC 3490; the new text says implementations MUST convert all U-labels to A-labels.
sections.plainLanguage: A certificate can only write names in plain letters, so a name in another alphabet is turned into a code starting with "xn--". Programs compare these codes letter for letter, and show people the nice version on screen.

sections.title: Name Constraints for Email
sections.content:
A name constraint limits which names a certification authority may issue certificates for. The update to Section 4.2.1.10 removes the ability to constrain a particular mailbox, such as the complete address of one account. The RFC says this capability was not used, and removing it lets name constraints apply to email addresses in both rfc822Name and SmtpUTF8Mailbox within otherName.

What remains is two forms. A constraint of the host name, for example example.com, is satisfied by any mail address at that host. A constraint with a leading period, for example .example.com, matches all mail addresses in the domain but not addresses on the host example.com itself.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a rule that says a school may only hand out ID cards for its own classrooms. You can say "everyone in this room" or "everyone in this hallway", but you can no longer say "just this one kid".

sections.title: Internationalized Email Addresses
sections.content:
Section 7.5 of RFC 5280 is replaced in full. Where an email address goes depends on its local-part (the part before the @). If the address includes an IDN but the local-part can be written in ASCII, the address goes in the rfc822Name choice of GeneralName, an IA5String. If the local-part cannot be written in ASCII, the address goes in SmtpUTF8Mailbox within otherName, following Section 3 of RFC 8398.

When the host-part contains an IDN, implementations MUST convert all U-labels to A-labels. Two addresses match when the local-parts match exactly and the host-parts match with a case-insensitive ASCII comparison. For the non-ASCII case, the UTF-8 encoding MUST NOT contain a Byte-Order-Mark, to aid comparison, and the local-part MUST conform to RFC 6530 and RFC 6531. As with domain names, a user interface SHOULD convert the host-part to Unicode before display.
sections.plainLanguage: Email addresses go in one of two boxes. If the part before the @ is plain letters, it goes in the ordinary box. If it has special letters, it goes in a special box built for that.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations for internationalized names in Section 4 of RFC 5890 apply. Conforming certification authorities SHOULD ensure that IDNs are valid according to IDNA2008. Failure to use valid A-labels may produce a domain name that cannot be correctly represented in the DNS.

The RFC repeats the lesson from RFC 8399: converting A-labels to U-labels to process name constraints for email in SmtpUTF8Mailbox led to implementation complexity and at least two security vulnerabilities, so now all IDNs are carried and processed as A-labels. It also points to the CA/Browser Forum guidance on internal server names in certificates. There are no IANA actions.
sections.plainLanguage: Switching spellings back and forth caused real bugs that attackers could use. Keeping one spelling all the way through is safer.
